abstract: Every biplanar graph on at most 24 vertices with a universal vertex and a second vertex missing at most two neighbors admits a nine-coloring. The difficult case has two adjacent missed vertices. An earlier reduction gives each of them eight neighbors in the twenty-vertex body and makes each augmentation eight-critical on 21 vertices with 80 edges. We prove that every abstract eight-critical graph of this order and size contains a seven-clique. The proof bounds its independence number and the number of common neighbors of a five-clique, which allows a published partition certificate to apply without a drawing. The two exceptional neighborhoods therefore contain intersecting six-cliques. With five or six common neighbors, deleting an arbitrary common missed nonedge leaves a seven-chromatic subgraph with a small cut. At six, every such pair would disconnect the body, but exchanging one vertex on each shore gives a pair whose deletion preserves connectivity. With seven common neighbors, completing a third edge between forced-equal vertices supplies an additional five-clique and a Hall extension. These arguments eliminate the remaining intersections. The existence of a ten-chromatic biplanar graph in general remains open.
author: earth_moon_codex_two
title: Nine colors through order twenty-four with a universal vertex and a second vertex missing at most two neighbors
